nameStory: This jumping spider carries the name 'grenada' likely referring to the Caribbean island of Grenada, though it's actually found in the southeastern United States. The genus name Hentzia honors Nicholas Marcellus Hentz, a 19th-century French-American naturalist who was one of the first to seriously study North American spiders. Like other members of its genus, it's called a 'long-jawed jumping spider' for the elongated chelicerae (jaws) that distinguish it from typical jumping spiders.
description: The Hentzia grenada is a small jumping spider with the characteristic large forward-facing eyes and compact, athletic build typical of its family. These spiders are active hunters that stalk and pounce on prey rather than building webs to catch food. With only 9 recorded observations in New England, this is an extremely rare find in our region, as it's primarily a southeastern species. Like all jumping spiders, it moves with quick, jerky motions and can leap several times its body length.

idTips.label: Eyes
idTips.description: Four large, dark eyes arranged in a row across the front of the face, with the middle pair noticeably larger and giving an almost cartoonish appearance - these eyes will seem to track your movement

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Compact, stocky build with a relatively flat, rectangular cephalothorax (front body section) that feels firm if gently touched - not the round, soft abdomen of orb weavers

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Moves in quick, stop-and-go jerks like a tiny robot, often turning to face you directly and appearing curious rather than fleeing immediately

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Small spider that could comfortably sit on a dime, with legs that don't extend much beyond a penny's diameter

idTips.label: Web
idTips.description: No web for catching prey - instead look for small silk retreats under bark or stones that feel like tiny sleeping bags

habitat: Given its extreme rarity in New England, likely found in the warmest microclimates such as south-facing rocky outcrops, sunny woodland edges, or areas near buildings that retain heat. In its native southeastern range, it prefers warm, dry locations with plenty of small prey insects. Any New England sighting would most likely be in southern Connecticut or Rhode Island in protected, sun-warmed spots.

seasonality.spring: If present, adults would become active as temperatures warm, emerging from winter retreats to hunt on sunny days when small flies and gnats are active.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period in its native range, when mating displays and egg-laying occur - any New England sighting would most likely happen during the warmest summer months.
seasonality.fall: Adults may remain active during warm autumn days, but would begin seeking protected overwintering sites as temperatures drop.
seasonality.winter: Inactive, sheltering under bark, stones, or other protected locations - extremely unlikely to be observed during New England winters.

funFact: Jumping spiders have better color vision than most mammals, including humans - they can see into the ultraviolet spectrum, meaning the world looks completely different to them than it does to us, with flowers and other objects displaying patterns we can't even imagine!
confusionNotes: Most likely to be confused with other small jumping spiders in the region, but the four large front eyes arranged in a straight row immediately identify it as a jumping spider rather than any other spider family. Memory trick: 'Four eyes forward, jumping spider' - no other spider family has this distinctive eye arrangement.
contextualKnowledge: This species represents a biogeographical puzzle - its presence in New England is so rare that each sighting is scientifically significant and may represent either natural range expansion due to climate change or accidental transport by humans. Any confirmed sighting should be reported to local naturalist groups.
compareHints: Hentzia grenada differs from its relatives the White-jawed Jumping Spider and Common Hentz Jumping Spider primarily in its extremely limited New England range and specific habitat preferences. All Hentzia species share the elongated jaws that give the genus its 'long-jawed' common name, distinguishing them from the more common bold jumping spiders that have shorter, more typical chelicerae.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among its Hentzia relatives, the white-jawed jumping spider is distinguished primarily by its namesake white jaw coloration, which is much more pronounced than in the Common Hentz jumping spider.
Compared to its relative the White-jawed Jumping Spider, the Common Hentz tends to be more brownish rather than having obvious white markings around the mouth area.
